Can the world withstand another winter of war? Submitted by Marco Carnelos on Mon, 11/02/2026 - 17:47 Amid ongoing conflicts in Ukraine and Iran, economic pressures are soaring around the globe High gas prices are displayed at a Shell station in Burbank, California, on 11 May 2026 (Mario Tama/Getty Images/AFP) Off Almost five years after the Russian invasion of Ukraine scrambled Europe’s energy map, another war has delivered a second shock. Since the US-Israeli war on Iran began this past February, the Strait of Hormuz, through which about a fifth of the world’s oil normally flows, has been closed or contested, while Ukraine’s drone campaign against Russian refineries has removed more fuel from an overstretched market. Increased energy prices feed inflation, forcing central banks to tighten monetary policy, while fiscal anxiety pushes up sovereign bond yields, inflating debt service. The final squeeze arrives in supply chains and households, and then in the streets and at the ballot boxes. In other words, it is a perfect storm - the mother of all perfect storms. We are seeing a clear example of historian Adam Tooze’s polycrisis concept: a situation where multiple, distinct crises overlap, amplifying their collective effects. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); The Iran war is the larger shock. Within days of its start, Brent crude jumped almost 19 percent to nearly $111 a barrel, from about $70 before the war. Washington called it “a very small price to pay” for security. After some ups and downs over the summer, oil was at $117 late last month . The International Energy Agency has called it the worst energy crisis in history. Even EU chief Ursula von der Leyen, the queen of denial, acknowledged “a regional conflict with unintended consequences”. Talks and periods of ceasefire have not normalised energy flows. The EU Commission has warned of a prolonged supply shock , which could involve forced cuts to fuel consumption before winter. Weak point To make a bad situation worse, the Houthis’ control over Yemen ’s Red Sea shores has endangered another chokepoint, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, with serious repercussions for maritime logistics. Compounding this, Ukraine’s attacks on Russian refineries have pushed Moscow into unprecedented export bans at the worst possible time, with the Iran war having already drained inventories. Europe no longer buys Russian diesel directly, but Russia’s former customers now compete for the same alternative cargoes. Hormuz drives most of the disruption, and the Russia-Ukraine war compounds it; together, they strike at the same weak point - a European continent that imports almost all of its fossil fuels. Governments in Paris, Rome and elsewhere have less fiscal space to compensate the public - and the combination of austerity and inflation is historically combustible The inevitable outcome has been inflation in the EU , which reached 3.8 percent in September, up from 3.2 percent in August - significantly higher than the rate of 2.6 percent a year prior. Food prices have also soared , fuelling widespread public anger in European cities. The European Central Bank’s president, Christine Lagarde, warned this summer that “the full inflationary impact of the energy shock has yet to play out”. Raising interest rates against a supply shock does nothing for commodity supplies, but it increases financing costs at exactly the moment when governments are being asked to cushion households. The bond market has noticed , with the yield on 30-year US Treasury bonds exceeding five percent this year, as national debt rose past $40 trillion and annual interest payments over $1 trillion for the first time. In the UK , 30-year yields recently hit six percent , the first time a G7 member had faced such rates since the 2012 eurozone crisis. France is at the epicentre of this crisis. Its bond yields stood at 4.85 percent in mid-October, near their highest levels in more than two decades, with EU officials urging Paris to present a credible budget. French debt service is projected at about €59 billion ($66bn) this year, compared with roughly €30 billion for Germany , and Italy must roll over debt worth 17 percent of GDP in 2026. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Ratchet turning This is not yet a replay of the 2011 economic crisis. Earlier in the war, analysts noted that Italian, Spanish and Greek yields stood below their 2022-23 peaks, because those countries had cut primary deficits. It’s important to note that debt offices feel higher yields only as maturing paper is replaced - so the bill grows with every auction, rather than arriving all at once. In economic jargon, it’s a ratchet, and each turn leaves less budgetary room for governments to offer the relief that angry households are demanding - even as these same governments continue to spend billions on arming Ukraine and launching unprecedented weapons procurement programmes. Dire social consequences arrived last month. In France, hundreds of thousands of people joined demonstrations that began as student protests over education, and widened into cost-of-living grievances. In Belgium, police clashed with protesters in Brussels, while tens of thousands of people marched in Lisbon, Portugal, over living costs, low wages and housing. Large and violent demonstrations were also reported in Italy. There does not seem to be a single Europe-wide movement, or at least not yet. Situations and demands differ by country, but ongoing economic shocks have served as an accelerant. France’s presidential election and Italy’s general election are both due next year, while Spain faces a snap election this month . EU governments are weighing support for vulnerable households, but disputes over the €2 trillion EU budget risk blocking decisions. With debt service rising, governments in Paris, Rome and elsewhere have less fiscal space to compensate the public - and the combination of austerity and inflation is historically combustible. US midterms The same energy shocks are now testing Donald Trump in Tuesday’s midterm elections, with the US president’s approval rating at a record low. About seven in 10 Americans say gasoline has become unaffordable, with the national average price above $4 a gallon for a record 158 days this year. Trump’s partial or total defeat - losing only the House, or losing both the House and the Senate - could trigger another constitutional crisis, like the one that occurred on 6 January 2021 , with Trump and his supporters refusing to accept a negative result. This all seems like a single feedback loop, rather than separate crises. A war of choice against Iran, backed by a US naval blockade, disrupts the Gulf; the price is paid first by importers in Europe and Asia, and then by American drivers; central banks respond with higher rates; bond markets reprice the debts of the most exposed states; and governments with shrinking fiscal space face electorates that have lost patience. The resilience of the world economy is built on illusion - it's time the West woke up Read More » The irony is that two crises aimed at inflicting a strategic defeat, and ideally regime change, in both Russia and Iran, have blown up in the faces of western liberal democracies, which are facing unbearable and dangerous costs. While Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has unsuccessfully tried to reduce US bond yields, further fuelling investors’ concerns , Trump has been scrambling to find a way to end the conflict in Ukraine , aiming to better focus on his war against Iran after the midterms. It is not clear yet whether Russia, Iran, and above all China will allow him such room for manoeuvre. Several crucial issues must now be monitored closely for developments, including the outcome of Israel ’s elections, which resulted in a deadlock last week; will the incoming government continue to bamboozle the US into waging an unnecessary war against Iran? Ongoing European economic negotiations will also be vital to watch, alongside the outcome of Tuesday’s US midterm vote and the impacts on markets and investments. In addition, what happens next in relation to the chokepoints at Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb will be crucial: if commodity flows normalise, prices could drop within months, and the storm may lose its force. If not, winter will be the next stress test - and it is fast approaching. The bullet had lodged in her lung. After a week in hospital, she died from her injuries. For her grandmother, Safia Abo Amra, Bayouk - the sole survivor of her immediate family in an earlier Israeli air strike - was far more than a granddaughter. She had become her closest companion and the centre of her life. “Fatima was my best friend. We did everything together, cooking, going on walks; we even slept on the same mattress. Concerned for her safety, Abo Amra refused to send her to a UN school after hearing that Israeli stray bullets frequently reached the area. Instead, she paid monthly fees to enrol her in a local school. “I walked Fatima to school every day. She was very smart and always did her homework before playing,” Abo Amra said. Her death reopened the grandmother’s wounds. “I was shocked and couldn't speak or move. Block on equality Which is the missing historical context for understanding the furore provoked by the Palestinian minority's surprise performance in last week’s election, gaining a record 19 seats in the 120-seat parliament. Palestinian “citizens” are only too aware that the wide support among Israeli Jews for their forced expulsion could all too quickly be translated into policy For many decades, the Palestinian minority’s vote in Israeli general elections steadily declined as the community understood that voting would make no difference to their own situation or that of the Palestinians under occupation. In fact, the more vocal Palestinian parties became in demanding equal rights, or highlighting Israel’s apartheid character - which they have managed to do with greater success in the age of social media - the more Israel’s Jewish parties agreed that the Palestinian minority were a threat to Israel’s image as a "Jewish and democratic" state. Over the past 20 years, the right and far-right, particularly Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party, have been the chief beneficiaries of that backlash. They have turned the tide in their favour with their racist incitement against the Palestinian minority. A 2025 poll showed a majority of Israeli Jews want Palestinian "citizens" forcibly expelled from the state. That is not because there is any tangible evidence the Palestinian minority poses a security threat. Rather, Israeli Jews fear that the minority’s higher birth rate will gradually erode the current Jewish majority, reversing 80 years of rigged demographics. The minority’s votes could then put it in a position to demand equal rights and launch a campaign to overturn Israel’s apartheid, just as South Africa’s black majority succeeded in doing to apartheid there more than 30 years ago. Netanyahu’s politically active son, Yair, made this point last week after the results were announced. He described the Palestinian minority as the "greatest threat to the survival of the State of Israel", aside from a supposed Iranian nuclear threat. It was for this reason that Netanyahu and the far-right pushed through the 2018 Basic Law : Israel as the Nation-State of the Jewish People, which formally declared that only the Jewish people have sovereignty in an expansive and undefined "Land of Israel". The move was largely in reaction to the increasing outspokenness of the Palestinian parties in challenging Israel’s claim to be a "Jewish and democratic" state. The Palestinian minority has long campaigned for Israel to become "a state of all its citizens" - that is, a liberal democracy. Efforts to advance such legislation in the Knesset have faced a fierce backlash from Israeli politicians and the courts. The main purpose of the Nation State Law is to provide a constitutional block on any attempt by the Palestinian parties to gain equal rights. Central fault line From Israel’s creation, the central fault line in its politics has been between the Jewish majority, on the one hand, and the Palestinian minority, on the other. Jewish parties disagree on individual policies, but they are unified on one thing: that the Palestinian parties, as well as the electorate they represent, are pariahs. They must be deprived of influence at all costs. Jewish parties disagree on individual policies, but they are unified on one thing: that the Palestinian parties, as well as the electorate they represent, are pariahs But in recent years, as Netanyahu has won election after election, the growing political clout of the Jewish far-right and religious right has opened up an additional fissure - this one within the Jewish majority, and largely unrelated to the Palestinian minority. After so long in power, the current far-right coalition is deeply corrupt. Netanyahu himself is currently on trial for fraud , bribery and breach of trust. Meanwhile, his government relies on the support of religious extremists who are intolerant, even contemptuous, of Israel’s secular Jewish public. And the far right’s flaunting of its fascist sympathies has, in the eyes of the traditional secular elites, irreparably damaged Israel’s image around the world. The Jewish majority is now irreconcilably divided . Although they are largely agreed on matters relating to the treatment of Palestinians - not least on the Gaza genocide - the pro-Netanyahu and anti-Netanyahu blocs can find little other common ground. They are especially at odds on the question of which kind of Jew - secular or religious - should be in control of a “Jewish” state. In effect, there is a low-level Jewish civil war going on in Israel that would probably have torn the country apart by now were it not for the fact that oppressing and abusing Palestinians - and neighbouring Arab states - serves as the glue holding Israel’s Jewish public together. The electoral difficulty for the Jewish majority is that their two hostile internal camps are evenly split. Half are deeply loyal to Netanyahu; the other half deeply opposed to him. That has left the Palestinian parties in an invidious position. They now hold the balance of power in parliament - earning them unwelcome kingmaker status. Genocidal logic There is a reason why so many Palestinian "citizens" turned out to vote at this election, despite their utter disillusionment with the Jewish majority. First, although there is an overwhelming consensus among Israeli Jews in support of the Gaza genocide, the Palestinian minority hopes that the opposition parties, unlike Netanyahu and his allies, are more likely to feel constrained in their actions by concerns about Israel’s image abroad. Netanyahu’s dependence on the support of unapologetic fascists in his coalition, such as Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich and National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir, means too that his government is more likely to expand the genocidal logic inherent in Zionism, on full display in Gaza, to the Palestinian minority next. Palestinian "citizens" are only too aware that the wide support among Israeli Jews for their forced expulsion could all too quickly be translated into policy. The founding ideology of so-called "liberal Zionism" may have fashioned Israel as a Jewish apartheid state, but Netanyahu and the far-right have shown they can push that ideology even further, into the darkest realms of human behaviour. The Palestinian minority turned out en masse to try to curb these excesses as best it could by lowering the overall proportion of votes for the Netanyahu bloc, keeping him further away from a majority, and thereby bolstering the opposition bloc. Unusually, the Palestinian parties have taken the difficult course of agreeing from the outset that they are willing to enter talks to support the opposition bloc, most likely from outside the government, even though they know the opposition can be expected to continue advancing Israel’s genocidal conduct in Gaza. Jockeying for power But what the Palestinian parties are learning for the umpteenth time is that the opposition camp, however worried it is by Netanyahu’s continuing rule, fears it would be even more dangerous to allow Palestinian "citizens" even a small degree of influence in the "Jewish" state. Netanyahu’s Likud party may have lost votes in the election but the Israeli right is still very much in the ascendant. Of the 120 Knesset seats, 93 went to hardline religious, ultra-nationalistic or militaristic factions . The leader of the opposition, Gadi Eisenkot, is a military general and father of the infamous Dahiya Doctrine of indiscriminately bombing and levelling the urban spaces of Israel’s neighbours - central to Israel’s strategy both in the Gaza genocide and in its onslaught on southern Lebanon. Eisenkot’s allies in the opposition bloc include Avigdor Lieberman, a far-right, secular politician who makes Netanyahu look like a moderate, and Naftali Bennett, who shares the religious Zionist ideology of the West Bank’s illegal settlers and was once a close ally of Netanyahu’s. Even the slightly more centrist Democrat party of Yair Golan , which won just eight seats, has equivocated over the creation of a Palestinian state, with Golan calling recent moves to recognise Palestine by Britain, Canada and France “a destructive move for Israel's security”. Whatever the eventual ruling coalition, there is no Jewish partner to be found in Israeli politics for the two-state solution that western capitals have been backing ever more frantically, supposedly as their contribution to ending Israel’s dispossession and slaughter of the Palestinian people. More likely, parts of the opposition may already be considering joining Netanyahu inside a Jewish unity government, setting aside their personal antipathies with him, rather than engage meaningfully with the Palestinian parties. Eisenkot is reported to have imposed conditions for what he has called a "broad Zionist government" - conditions he knows the Palestinian parties cannot accept, including recognising Israel as a "Jewish and democratic state" and declaring Hamas a terrorist organisation. He has alleged , without evidence of course, that the Palestinian parties "stole" the election. A statement from his Likud party last week described the Palestinian parties’ electoral success as "a terror attack on democracy meant to lead to a foreign takeover of the Knesset [and] the Islamization of Israel”. Moshe Feiglin, one of Netanyahu’s allies, demanded that Israel hold fresh elections, this time with paramilitary police forces stationed at polling stations that serve Palestinian “citizens”. Channel 14 TV dubbed the Palestinian parties’ success the "Ballot Box Terror Affair". As an editorial in the liberal Haaretz newspaper observed : "Arab citizens have spent four years being treated as enemies by the national security minister [Ben Gvir]. Now, Netanyahu is trying to make their most basic right - the right to vote - into a crime." Zionism is racism As western media pore over the fallout from the election, it is easy to overlook the big picture. Netanyahu, wanted by the International Criminal Court (ICC) for crimes against humanity in starving Gaza’s population, won the largest share of the vote last week. He is still Israel’s most popular politician. Any government that might emerge from the current post-election talks - even were it to be supported by the Palestinian parties - would be dominated by the extreme right. An opposition-led coalition will be no less hawkish and vehemently hostile to the Palestinians, whether those under occupation or those with Israeli “citizenship”, than a Netanyahu-led one. Although this was the first election since Israel launched its genocidal rampage through Gaza in late 2023, debate about the genocide was absent from the campaign trail - as was talk of the intensifying pogroms by settler terrorists on Palestinian communities in the West Bank. Channel 12 invited into its studios a representative sample of these 18- to 21-year-olds. Out of 12, 11 answered that they were against Palestinian parties being allowed to sit in the parliament – let alone join a government. These new voters are gradually shifting Israeli politics ever further to the far right. This election was stark confirmation that Britain’s Green party was decisively right to adopt a new policy last month at its conference that declared Zionism - the political ideology underpinning Israel as a Jewish state - to be racist. It was the warped logic of Zionism, not some need for security, that propelled Israel into levelling Gaza and killing and maiming many tens of thousands of Palestinian children. MOTORSPORT: CATCHING THE DRIFT. Laiba Khan Lodhi | Instagram/@laibakhanlodhi101 In 2024, Laiba Khan Lodhi posted a video of herself doing donuts in her Mercedes, a skill she had learned at the Pro Drift Academy Dubai. The video caught the attention of the local street-racing community, and someone made a meme out of it, making fun of the young female driver. All sorts of negative comments, such as “Women belong in the kitchen” and “Leave driving to the boys” along with teacup emojis, abuse and threats, started pouring in. It disappointed her. At the same time, it fueled her passion, motivating her to adopt drifting as a career. “The attitude behind those comments implied that motorsports somehow was a property of men only — I wanted to challenge that,” Laiba says while talking to Eos. “I knew I couldn’t change everyone’s mind, but I could prove that women belong on the track too.” Mocked in a meme and flooded with misogynistic online comments over an early car drifting video, Laiba Khan Lodhi used that negativity to fuel her drive to become a professional drifter Drifting is a type of motorsport in which the car must slide sideways in an oversteer condition — such as the rear-wheel slip during cornering — and be controlled by the drivers. Competitors are judged based on their drifting skill and manoeuvring, and drivers must demonstrate speed and control of the drift. When she asked her parents to allow her to pursue drifting professionally, they did not hinder her. In fact, they restored her confidence and encouraged her to prove her detractors wrong. “Their support has meant a lot, especially at a time when so many people were trying to discourage me,” she says. GROWING UP WITH CARS Cars have always been a part of Laiba’s life. Her father owned a car business in Islamabad and would often bring different vehicles home, sometimes wanting her to be the first to drive them. From convertibles to classic cars, she grew up experiencing all kinds of rides and gradually developed an emotional attachment to them. “I get attached to cars very easily,” she admits. “I still remember the cars I’ve sat in, and I’ve even cried when we sold a few of them.” Still, a career behind the wheel was never part of her life plan. Her ambitions kept changing as she grew up. At one point, she wanted to join the army and, later, she considered becoming a pilot. Though her career aspirations had always been adventurous, drifting never crossed her mind. Then came the meme, and it changed everything. Lodhi behind the wheel THE CHALLENGE OF DRIFTING Instead of retreating under social pressure, Laiba took it as a challenge to the stereotype, reflecting her strong personality. By 2026, Laiba had become a household name in Pakistan’s drifting and racing community, earning over a million followers on Instagram, with drifting videos garnering millions of views. Drifting is not cheap, and Laiba knew that when she chose it. You need a well-maintained car, you pay for tracks, and you spend on training. To bear her expenses and grow as an individual, she creates content around cars, collaborates with brands and also runs a modest-wear brand, Ajwa Modest Wear. “I have even bought [drifting] cars with my own money, which makes me proud. Being financially independent matters a lot to me,” she says. Her hard work and skill have gained her some international exposure. Earlier this year, in January, she competed in the Saudi Toyota Drift Championship in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, where she was the only female drifter and the sole representative of Pakistan. THE FIRST ACCIDENT Then came a different kind of test. Looking to push her limits and conquer other tracks, Laiba competed in the Cholistan Desert Rally in the Women’s Prepared Category, venturing into unfamiliar territory. It was a tough but memorable experience, as she had her first accident while driving. She got off to a difficult start when she hit a tree, damaging the side mirror and front windscreen, but carried on. Later, she could not spot a pothole in time, and the impact hurt her arm so badly that paramedics had to check on her. “It was a lot to go through in my first race, but I consider it an important experience,” she says. “Motorsport always carries risks, and that day reminded me how much proper preparation and safety matter. I was proud that I finished, and even came away with a podium [finish].” Laiba Khan Lodhi has come a long way from the girl who faced online hate. Today, people tell her they are proud of her, and parents say their daughters want to try drifting, too. “Hearing that makes me really happy,” she gushes. “I feel that by showing up and continuing, I have helped make the sport feel more possible for other women.” The writer is a communication specialist and a freelance sports journalist Published in Dawn, EOS, November 1st, 2026

Following the revision, petrol will retail at Rs374.51 per litre, while HSD will cost Rs395.20. The prices are applicable for Nov 3 (Tuesday), according to a notification by the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra). The government continues to levy Rs114 per litre in taxes and duties on petrol and Rs100 per litre on diesel. However, under a new arrangement , oil refineries would contribute to the petroleum levy by bearing a monthly cumulative impact of Rs15 billion, according to the government. This would allow a Rs14.71 reduction in the petrol price on consumers’ end. “The [petroleum levy] impact on estimated total country volume of Rs. 14.71/litre shall be surrendered by refineries @ Rs49.02/litre on their sales to [oil marketing companies],” reads a document by Ogra. The government announced the arrangement during a press conference in Islamabad, held by Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik and Information Minister Attaullah Tarar. “I am grateful to all the refineries that saw the public is in difficulty and with the government’s help … increased their throughput,” Malik said, adding that these refineries had made profits from this throughput in the last three months. “They were requested to take a step to support the public during this difficult time, and I am glad that they listened to us … the Rs15 increase that was coming in the petrol prices on Friday, they helped the government with that. Because of that, we were able to maintain the price.” On Oct 27, Jamaat-i-Islami (JI) chief Hafiz Naeemur Rehman met with Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif in Islamabad to discuss his party’s demand to provide relief to the public by abolishing the levy. The two sides agreed to form a joint committee of the JI and the government to consider the expansion of the ongoing fuel relief scheme , being offered to owners of motorcycles, rickshaws and vehicles of up to 800cc since Sept 17 . For his part, Rehman declared that his party would march to Islamabad in protest of the petroleum levy in mid-November if the government did not announce any major relief by then. Rise in fuel prices The price of HSD has come down from a peak of Rs520.35 recorded on April 3. Its price had started rising from Rs281 per litre after the US-Iran war broke out on Feb 28. The petrol price had peaked at Rs458.41 on April 3 after beginning its upward trajectory from Rs266 in the first week of March. Meanwhile, the government has reintroduced a raft of austerity measures in response to rising fuel prices amid the ongoing Middle East conflict. Under these measures, markets are required to close by 9pm, and fuel allocations for official vehicles have been cut by 50 per cent for three months. On Sept 13, PM Shehbaz also announced a “ relief scheme ” for users of motorcycles, autos and vehicles of up to 800cc to “alleviate the burden” of rising global oil prices. Previously, on July 17, the petroleum minister announced that fuel prices would now be fixed on a daily basis due to fluctuations in international market prices following renewed hostilities between Iran and the US. Prior to this, the government had been announcing weekly revisions to fuel prices since early March, alongside measures for the conservation of fuel amid possible oil supply disruptions due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. The federal government in April also announced targeted relief measures to provide subsidised fuel. The petroleum minister stated that the cabinet and the prime minister had decided to give Ogra the responsibility of deciding fuel prices on a daily basis based on international market trends. Petrol is mainly used in private transport, small vehicles, rickshaws and two-wheelers, and changes in its price affect the middle and lower-middle classes. Similarly, changes in diesel prices also impact the public at large, as it is mainly used in the heavy transport sector, power plants and large generators. Petrol and HSD are the major revenue earners, with monthly sales of about 700,000 to 800,000 tonnes, compared to just 10,000 tonnes of monthly demand for kerosene. Additional input by Khaleeq Kiani

Taliban govt voices concern over US plans for deportation. KABUL: Afghanistan’s Taliban authorities voiced concern on Monday over reported plans by Washington to deport scores of Afghan immigrants to Pakistan with the aim of their eventual return to their home country. More than 150 Afghans in the United States would be deported via Pakistan to Afghanistan, including relatives of those who assisted US forces before their 2021 withdrawal, according to US media reports and an advocacy group. “The Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan expresses its serious concern over reports that the United States intends to deport some Afghan refugees to Pakistan who have not yet been able to obtain legal residency documents in that country,” foreign ministry spokesman Abdul Qahar Balkhi said in a statement. Advocacy groups have warned that the removal of former allies and their families could endanger their lives. After regaining power, Taliban authorities announced a general amnesty for Afghans who worked with Western-backed forces and governments and have repeated promises this year that their former foes could safely return home. However, the United Nations has recorded reports of extrajudicial killings, detentions and abuses. President Donald Trump’s administration last year issued travel bans for a number of countries, including Afghanistan, as part of a broad immigration crackdown. His administration sought to end deportation protections for Afghans, some of whom were granted special immigrant visas following the 2021 takeover by Taliban authorities. Govt seeks PPP, MQM nominees for electoral reforms panel. ISLAMABAD: Taking ownership of an initiative to bring all parliamentary parties, including the opposition, to the negotiating table on electoral reforms, the government on Monday formally appr­oached its allies to join the proposed Parliamentary Committee on Electoral Reforms (PCER). The government contacted its key allies, the PPP and the MQM, seeking nominations for their representatives on the proposed committee. The PPP has submitted the names of its legislators for the PCER. However, the names have not yet been made public. Federal Minister for Par­liamentary Affairs Tar­iq Fazal Chaudhry wrote separate letters to the chief whips of the PPP and MQM in the National Ass­embly, Ijaz Jakhrani and Aminul Haq, respectively, seeking nominations for the committee. Talking to Dawn , Mr Chaudhry said National Assembly Speaker Sardar Ayaz Sadiq had received the names from the PPP. However, he said the government would announce the names of all committee members at a later stage. He said the ruling PML-N would have nine members, while the PPP would have five and the MQM one. Explaining the formula for representation of parliamentary parties on the committee, the minister said one member would be allocated for every 16 members of the National Assembly. He said that, under the agreed criteria, smaller parties allied with the ruling coalition did not qualify for representation on the committee. The PML-N had therefore decided to allocate one seat each to its smaller allies, including the Balochistan Awami Party (BAP) and Pakistan Muslim League-Zia (PML-Z), from its own quota of nine seats. Asked whether the government would also directly approach the opposition to seek nominations for the committee, Mr Chaudhry said the PPP had already contacted opposition parties and that they were now required to submit the names of their representatives directly to the National Assembly speaker. The parliamentary affairs minister clarified that the initiative to form the committee had been taken by Speaker Sardar Ayaz Sadiq, not the PPP. He said he would begin meeting parliamentary leaders of all parties from today (Tuesday) to obtain nominations for the electoral reforms committee. Mr Chaudhry said there was no reason to believe that the PML-N-led government would not complete its five-year constitutional term. He added that the PPP had met opposition leaders at the initiative of the National Assembly speaker. “The PPP can only meet opposition leaders as a political move, but the party has no mandate to do anything else,” he said. Responding to a question, Mr Chaudhry acknowledged that the PPP was creating difficulties for the government in legislative business. “The PPP is pinching us in making legislation, but the party cannot keep itself away from the system,” he said. He insisted that the opposition should join the parliamentary committee, saying the initiative would open the door to consultations on other important national issues. Imported wheat fails to cut flour prices. KARACHI: Although the arrival of imported wheat has brought down prices in the open market, consumers continue to pay high prices for different varieties of flour and Roti. On Oct 28, when the first ship carrying 51,000 tonnes of wheat berthed at the port, wheat prices in the open market plunged to Rs130 from Rs140 per kilogram. Another ship carrying 58,132 tonnes is due at Karachi today (Tuesday). Wheat prices in the open market started fluctuating in the open market after arrival of the imported grain. Market stakeholders quoted different rates. According to wholesalers, the average price stood at Rs132 per kg, while millers say that rates hovered between Rs136 and Rs137 per kg. Millers had raised the prices of different varieties of flour by Rs20 per kg, but later brought down prices ahead of the arrival of imported wheat. A miller claimed that all the mills had reduced prices on Oct 28, two days ahead of the ship’s arrival. The latest mill prices of flour No 2.5, Maida and fine flour are Rs156, Rs168 and Rs171, respectively, while the rates during the first week of October were Rs161, Rs173 and Rs176, respectively. No relief for consumer But consumers have yet to get any relief as the rates for Chapati, Naan, Sheermal/Taftaan and Qulcha remain unchanged at Rs20, Rs30-35, Rs100-110 and Rs90-100, respectively. A tandoor owner said the high price of liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) (Rs500-550 per kg) has offset the impact of reduction in flour prices. “It will be hard to sustain our operations in case LPG prices go up further,” he said. Likewise, the retail rates for flour No 2.5 and Maida remained unchanged at Rs170-180 and Rs185-190, while fine flour sold Rs185-190 per kg. Rauf Ibrahim, a wholesaler, said the regulator has been unable to check inflated retail rates despite a dip in the open market. He said the import of 750,000 tonnes of wheat will turn out to be insufficient as the country needs over two million tonnes to bridge the demand and supply gap as the new crops from Sindh and Punjab will arrive only between March and May. Ibrahim urged the government to allow the private sector and flour millers to import grain in order to stabilise flour prices. He said the lives of workers earning below Rs50,000 have become miserable since they have to spend almost the entire income on putting food on the table, leaving little for their children’s education and other needs. Disparity in prices Consumers living in Karachi and Hyderabad are paying the highest prices for flour varieties compared to other cities across the country. As per the Sensitive Price Index (SPI) ending Oct 29, a 20kg flour bag in Karachi costs up to Rs3,540 while its average price in other parts of the country is Rs3,200. Hyderabad holds the second spot where the price of a 20kg bag ranges between Rs3,360 and Rs3,400. In Islamabad, Rawa­lpindi, Lahore and other major Punjab cities, prices ranged between Rs2,200 and Rs3,333. Wheat rates Sukkur is much ahead in terms of wheat rates as a 10kg bag sells for Rs1,488, while Peshawar holds the second spot with a rate of Rs1,469. The third highest rate of Rs1,453 prevails in Hyderabad. In Karachi the 10kg bag is available at Rs1,440. In Islamabad and Rawalpindi, the average price is Rs1,453. The lowest rate for a 10kg bag is in Sargodha with Rs1,223, followed by Bahawalpur with Rs1,266 and Rs1,300 in Faisalabad and Sialkot. Fine Atta Consumers in Hyderabad and Quetta are paying the highest rate of Rs187 per kg, followed by Rs185 per kg being paid by the people of Karachi. The third highest rate of Rs183 per kg prevails in Islamabad. In other cities, the average price of one kilogram of fine flour ranged between Rs147 and Rs180 per kg. A flour miller said that one of the reasons for high prices in Karachi is that the city is not a wheat-growing area and is dependent on the arrival of grain from the rest of Sindh. JIT chief issued show cause over delay in submission of final charge sheet in Mir Raza murder case. KARACHI: A judicial magistrate on Monday issued a show-cause notice to DIG Irfan Baloch, chief of the newly formed joint investigation team (JIT) in the Mir Raza murder case, after police failed to submit the final charge sheet. He has been directed to respond by Nov 10. The Sindh home department had formed the JIT, led by DIG Baloch, on the recommendation of a single-member judicial commission comprising Justice Omar Sial of the Sindh High Court. The team was tasked with investigating the circumstances surrounding Mir Raza’s death and possible negligence in the case. Two previous high-level investigation teams had failed to identify the culprit or establish how Mir Raza’s body came to be found in mysterious circumstances. DSP Lashari is no longer IO in the case after formation of JIT, court told The then investigating officers (IOs) had sought three extensions to submit the final report, saying that they were awaiting forensic reports and a response from Apple company regarding Mir Raza’s mobile phone. Complainant’s counsel Daniyal Muhammad Hussain told Dawn that at Monday’s hearing the complainant’s side informed the court that DSP Sirajuddin Lashari was no longer the IO in the case as a JIT had been formed. He also submitted the official notification regarding the JIT’s formation. He added that no police official or JIT member appeared before the court, although the date had been fixed for submission of the final charge sheet. After a brief hearing, the magistrate asked the JIT head to explain why the charge sheet had not been submitted. DSP Lashari told this reporter that he had handed over the case file to the JIT head so the team could proceed with the investigation, adding that he was no longer the IO. Mir Raza, 25, a businessman, had gone missing on July 28 after leaving his home in PECHS. His body, bearing a gunshot wound, was found in bushes in Gulistan-i-Jauhar a day later. In his interim report, the IO named 63 witnesses but wrote “no one” in the column for the accused. In his conclusion, he stated that despite probing all possible angles, police had yet to find any clue or make a breakthrough. The report also contained detailed information about the case, from the registration of the FIR on the complaint of Mir Raza’s father after he went missing to the handover of the investigation to the JIT.
