Le général Abdel Fattah al-Bourhane, le chef de l’armée soudanaise, en garde toutefois une certaine rancune au président centrafricain Faustin-Archange Touadéra. 144 Entretiens de Crisis Group, sources gouvernementales et diplomates, Bangui, avril 2026. « Faustin-Archange Touadéra face au contrecoup de ses alliances au Soudan », Africa Intelligence , 5 juin 2025. Ce dernier, pour sa part, reproche au commandant soudanais de coopérer avec le chef rebelle centrafricain Nourredine Adam, qui dirige le FPRC. 145 Ibid. Les relations entre le président Touadéra et le général al-Bourhane sont réputées froides. 146 Ibid. Dès 2024, les autorités centrafricaines ont tenté de rééquilibrer leur position à l’égard des deux camps soudanais. Elles ont évité de collaborer officiellement avec les FSR, malgré leur présence le long de la frontière entre la RCA et le Soudan. Les paramilitaires soudanais, notamment le général Djazouli, ont pourtant proposé en 2024 aux forces centrafricaines d’établir une coopération formelle pour sécuriser la zone frontalière. 147 Entretiens de Crisis Group, sources sécuritaires, nord-est de la RCA, avril 2026. Prudent, Bangui a ouvert des discussions informelles pour permettre l’échange de renseignements et prévenir la circulation de miliciens soudanais dans la Vakaga, mais a refusé d’officialiser cette collaboration afin de ne pas légitimer les FSR. Parallèlement, le président Touadéra a participé, en 2024 puis en mai 2025, à plusieurs rencontres informelles avec des représentants du général al-Bourhane afin de réaffirmer la neutralité centrafricaine et de demander l’arrestation de Nourredine Adam lors de ses passages au Soudan. 148 « Sous l’œil d’Alger, Touadéra engagé dans un pas de deux avec Burhan », Africa Intelligence , 16 février 2024. Ces rencontres n’ont toutefois pas permis de rétablir la confiance entre les deux parties. 149 Entretiens téléphoniques de Crisis Group, sources confidentielles, avril 2026. « Faustin-Archange Touadéra face au contrecoup de ses alliances au Soudan », op. cit. B. L’irrésistible influence économique des EAU en RCA Depuis le début du conflit, le Soudan est devenu le théâtre de rivalités entre plusieurs puissances étrangères engagées aux côtés de l’un ou l’autre des deux belligérants. 150 « Sudan’s proxy war », Africa Defense Forum, 5 août 2025. L’Arabie Saoudite, l’Egypte et la Turquie soutiennent l’armée soudanaise, tandis que les EAU sont les principaux parrains des FSR. 151 Voir la déclaration de Crisis Group, « Sudan : A year of war », 11 avril 2024. Au-delà des considérations idéologiques (lutte contre les Frères musulmans et les réseaux islamistes liés à l’ancien régime d’Omar al-Bashir) et géostratégiques (contrôle de la mer Rouge) propres au Soudan, Abou Dhabi cherche à sécuriser un accès à des ressources stratégiques (produits agricoles, minerais), à contrôler des corridors commerciaux et à accroitre son influence géopolitique. Les EAU ont convaincu des pays limitrophes du Soudan, comme le Tchad et l’Ethiopie, de mettre leur territoire à disposition pour faciliter l’approvisionnement en armes des paramilitaires soudanais. 152 « Boeings identified in Reuters report carried weapons for Sudanese paramilitary », op. cit ; « Sudan’s civil war fueled by secret arms shipment from UAE and Iran », op. cit ; « Talking peace in Sudan, the U.A.E secretly fuels the fight », op. cit ; « Secretary of state Marco Rubio before the house foreign affairs committee on the FY27 department of state budget request », op. cit. ; et « The UAE in Africa: Power, influence and conflict », op. cit. Comme son voisin tchadien, la RCA pourrait à son tour se laisser entrainer plus activement dans les hostilités sous l’influence de son puissant partenaire émirati. L’éclatement de la guerre au Soudan a considérablement renforcé l’intérêt économique des EAU pour la RCA. 153 Avant 2023, les échanges entre les deux pays se confinaient au domaine commercial, en particulier dans le secteur aurifère, malgré plusieurs voyages du président Touadéra et de son cercle à Abou Dhabi et à Dubaï, en quête d’investissements et d’aides financières. Dubaï est la principale destination de l’or africain. Les autorités y sont peu regardantes sur l’origine du métal précieux, qui arrive par des circuits légaux ou informels. En 2022, le Financial Times estimait, sur la base de données agrégées, que 405 des 435 tonnes d’or exportées illégalement d’Afrique étaient destinées aux EAU. Pour plus d’informations, voir « The illegal gold rush sweeping the world », Financial Times , 20 août 2025 ; « Centrafrique : Sigma Mining, la discrète société émirienne au cœur de l’or centrafricain », Africa Intelligence , 18 mai 2026 ; « Comment Touadéra veut renflouer ses caisses avec des bitcoins de Dubaï », Africa Intelligence , 10 mai 2022. En juin 2023, International Holding Company (IHC) – un conglomérat présidé par Tahnoun Ben Zayed Al Nahyan, frère du président émirati Mohammed Ben Zayed Al Nahyane et conseiller à la sécurité nationale – a créé plusieurs sociétés à Bangui dans le secteur minier. Celles-ci sont depuis devenues des acteurs nationaux majeurs dans la cartographie, l’exploration, l’exploitation ou l’exportation de l’or. 154 Documents financiers consultés par Crisis Group, avril 2025. Entretiens téléphoniques de Crisis Group, sources confidentielles, mai 2025. Basé à Abou Dhabi, le groupe IHC est actif dans de nombreux secteurs, notamment l’énergie, l’agroalimentaire, l’immobilier, la santé et les services financiers. « International Holding Company PJSC - Review report and interim financial information », Abu Dhabi Securities Exchange, 6 novembre 2024. Ces entreprises achètent aussi d’importantes quantités d’or aux principaux bureaux d’achat centrafricains. 155 Les quatre sociétés créées à Bangui sont des joint-ventures avec l’Etat centrafricain et sont toutes détenues à 85 pour cent par IHC. Il s’agit de Sigma Ressource CAR 1, Sigma Ressource CAR 2, Sigma Mineral CAR et Sigma Gold CAR. Ces entreprises détiennent dix permis en RCA (dans le Mbomou, la Nana-Mambéré, la Ouaka et la Vakaga). Documents financiers consultés par Crisis Group, avril 2026. « Centrafrique : Sigma Mining, la discrète société émirienne au cœur de l’or centrafricain », op. cit. En 2024, le partenariat entre les deux pays s’est intensifié avec l’annonce d’importants investissements émiratis en RCA, notamment un projet de nouvel aéroport à Bangui, estimé à 200 millions de dollars (non encore financé), et la construction d’une centrale électrique d’un coût de 90 millions de dollars. 156 Abou Dhabi et Bangui ont encore approfondi leur coopération en mars 2025, avec la signature d’un accord de partenariat économique global par Mohammed Ben Zayed Al Nahyane et le président Touadéra. Cet accord vise à structurer et renforcer les relations économiques entre les deux pays, en facilitant les échanges commerciaux et en créant un cadre favorable à de futurs investissements, notamment dans des secteurs stratégiques comme l’agriculture, les infrastructures, la technologie et la logistique. Voir « Le président des Emirats et le président de la République centrafricaine assistent à la signature d’un accord de partenariat économique global », Emirates News Agency, 6 mars 2025 ; « La Centrafrique et les Emirats signent un accord pour la construction d’un nouvel aéroport à Bangui », RFI, 19 janvier 2024 ; « Centrafrique : 90 millions USD des Emirats arabes unis dans une centrale solaire de 60 MW », Financial Afrik , 18 août 2025. Le profil des opérateurs économiques émiratis en RCA témoigne d’une stratégie d’investissement coordonnée et pilotée par les autorités des EAU. 157 Documents financiers consultés par Crisis Group, avril 2026. La famille royale d’Abou Dhabi contrôle les sociétés aurifères mentionnées plus haut, tandis que la centrale électrique sera exploitée par Noor, une entreprise détenue par le consortium parapublic Abu Dhabi Power Corporation. En août 2025, un ressortissant des EAU a également créé Invicta Air Cargo, une société de fret aérien appartenant à une chaine de holdings détenues par Mohammed Ben Zayed Al Nahyane lui-même. 158 « Les Emirats arabes unis réorganisent leur réseau de livraisons d’armes aux paramilitaires soudanais », Le Monde , 19 mars 2026. Documents confidentiels consultés par Crisis Group en juin 2026. Ces investissements ont renforcé l’influence des EAU auprès des autorités de Bangui, confrontées à d’importants besoins de financement. 159 Les EAU disposent d’un fonds souverain dont les actifs dépassent les 1 500 milliards de dollars et ils investissent massivement en Afrique. « The UAE’s imperial push into Africa », Financial Times , 4 août 2026. Cette riche monarchie du Golfe, dont les dépenses publiques annuelles (nationales et fédérales) s’élèvent à environ 134 milliards de dollars, est devenu au cours de la dernière décennie l’un des premiers fournisseurs de capitaux en Afrique. 160 « Government Financial Statistics », ministère des Finances des EAU, consulté en octobre 2026. Elle possède des moyens démesurés par rapport à la RCA, dont le budget national annuel, parmi les plus modestes du continent africain, avoisine les 700 millions de dollars. 161 « Rapport d’exécution budgétaire au premier trimestre 2026 », ministère centrafricain des Finances et du Budget, 15 mai 2026. Fortes de leur influence grandissante en RCA, les autorités d’Abou Dhabi ont exploré la possibilité d’utiliser le territoire centrafricain pour livrer de l’équipement militaire aux FSR. Lors d’une visite officielle dans le pays en août 2025, une délégation émiratie s’est discrètement rendue à Birao et a manifesté un intérêt pour l’aéroport, ainsi que pour la construction, jamais annoncée officiellement, d’un hôpital dans cette même localité. 162 Entretiens de Crisis Group, sources confidentielles, nord-est de la RCA, avril 2026. Un terrain aurait été réservé à cet effet, mais les travaux n’ont pas encore démarré. 163 Cette configuration rappelle celle observée au Tchad. En 2023, Abou Dhabi avait financé la construction d’un hôpital à Amdjarass, une ville de l’est tchadien située à la frontière avec le Darfour, en même temps qu’il y faisait transiter des armes à destination des FSR. L’hôpital d’Amdjarass a soigné des paramilitaires soudanais blessés au combat. Des diplomates étrangers l’ont régulièrement décrit comme une couverture pour les livraisons d’armes. Le Tchad et les EAU démentent catégoriquement ces accusations. « Dozens of UAE flights head to airstrip UN says supplies arms to Sudan rebels », Reuters, 12 décembre 2024. Depuis 2023, des équipements et des combattants auraient transité par la RCA en direction du Soudan, mais toujours en faible volume et de manière ponctuelle. Certaines livraisons auraient été effectuées par Wagner (voir plus haut) ; d’autres proviendraient des EAU. Des témoins locaux et un officier des FSR à Nyala ont confié à Crisis Group que quelques cargaisons d’armes et de matériel envoyées par les EAU et destinées aux FSR auraient emprunté le territoire centrafricain entre 2024 et début 2026, avant de rejoindre Nyala. 164 Entretiens de Crisis Group, sources confidentielles, Vakaga et Nyala (Soudan), janvier-avril 2026. Le volume de ces livraisons reste dérisoire par rapport à celui transitant par d’autres pays frontaliers du Soudan. Pour l’instant, la RCA ne constitue donc pas un corridor logistique majeur, mais elle offre une solution de secours pour les EAU, alors que le Tchad a rencontré à plusieurs reprises des difficultés pour acheminer des armes aux FSR en raison de tensions politiques internes. 165 Entretiens de Crisis Group, sources confidentielles, septembre 2026. Le Soudan a menacé à plusieurs reprises de représailles les pays laissant transiter des armes pour le compte des FSR. Si le partenariat avec les EAU s’inscrit dans une politique bien établie de Bangui visant à diversifier ses partenariats internationaux, tant sur le plan sécuritaire qu’économique, il n’est pas sans risques. Le Soudan a menacé à plusieurs reprises de représailles les pays laissant transiter des armes pour le compte des FSR. En mars 2025, un général de l’armée soudanaise a affirmé que les aéroports tchadiens utilisés pour acheminer ces livraisons constituaient des « cibles légitimes ». 166 « Le Soudan menace d’attaquer les aéroports tchadiens », Deutsche Welle, 24 mars 2025. En août, le Tchad a accusé l’armée soudanaise d’avoir effectué un bombardement aérien sur son territoire, à plus de 100 kilomètres de la frontière entre les deux pays. 167 « Tchad : l’armée dénonce une incursion de plus de 100 km sur son territoire depuis le Soudan », Tchad Infos , 22 août 2026. Fulbert Ngodji, « Chad blames Sudan’s army for strikes on convoy », Analyst’s Notebook de Crisis Group, 28 août 2026. La RCA pourrait faire l’objet de menaces ou de représailles similaires si elle devenait à son tour une plateforme logistique importante pour les FSR. Pis, le partenariat avec les EAU ne protège pas pour autant le pays des violences commises par des individus associés aux FSR, comme en témoigne la situation dans la Vakaga, mais aussi au Tchad, qui connait lui aussi de fréquents incidents impliquant des paramilitaires soudanais. 168 « L’est du Tchad happé par la guerre au Soudan », op. cit. Pour Bangui, cependant, les bénéfices politiques et économiques immédiats de la collaboration avec les EAU semblent pour le moment l’emporter sur les risques qu’elle fait peser, à plus long terme, sur la sécurité du pays et sur ses relations avec le Soudan. V. Anticiper les dangers à venir Les répercussions de la guerre au Soudan constituent un défi de taille pour le fragile Etat centrafricain et pourraient remettre en cause les progrès sécuritaires enregistrés depuis l’accord de paix de Khartoum en 2019 et l’offensive des forces étatiques contre les groupes armés rebelles en 2021. Alors que les hostilités entre l’armée soudanaise et les FSR se poursuivent au Soudan, la circulation de combattants liés aux paramilitaires dans la préfecture de la Vakaga risque de s’accentuer, alimentée par les défections et les opportunités de pillage évoquées plus haut. 169 « Dissident RSF commander Savannah arrives in Khartoum », Sudan Tribune , 15 mai 2026 ; « In Sudan, RSF defections embolden SAF », Africa Defense Forum, 23 juin 2026. La RCA offre en outre aux FSR quittant le Soudan un cadre sans doute plus favorable que celui d’autres pays voisins, comme le Tchad, dotés d’un appareil sécuritaire plus robuste. L’intensification des frappes de drones par l’armée soudanaise au Darfour méridional pourrait aussi pousser davantage de miliciens à stationner en RCA, à l’abri des bombardements. 170 « Sudan army drone attack on Darfur kills 35, rights group says », Al Jazeera, 2 août 2026 ; « Strikes hit Sudan cities as army chief defiant after US visa snub », Arab News, 27 septembre 2026. Un surcroit d’éléments soudanais dans le nord-est de la RCA pourrait entrainer une nouvelle hausse de la criminalité, des entraves à la circulation des biens et des personnes, une militarisation des litiges socioéconomiques et des violences xénophobes contre les réfugiés soudanais. Cette instabilité pourrait aider les groupes armés centrafricains actifs dans le nord-est à restaurer leurs capacités financières et matérielles. Le FPRC et le PRNC – le premier n’ayant pas réintégré l’accord de 2019 et le second ayant été créé après sa signature – pourraient notamment profiter des rentes offertes par le conflit soudanais pour accroitre leurs recrutements. Des responsables du MPC, comme Algoni Tidjani, ont déjà rejoint la zone des trois frontières (entre le Tchad, le Soudan et la RCA) avec leurs hommes et participé, fin juin, à l’attaque contre Am-Dafock. 171 Entretiens téléphoniques de Crisis Group, représentants de groupes armés, avril 2026. S’ils continuent à se renforcer, les rebelles pourraient mener des attaques dans la Vakaga, occuper des villes ou des axes routiers et chercher à s’étendre aux préfectures limitrophes. Cette dynamique leur donnerait davantage de poids dans les négociations avec le gouvernement en vue d’obtenir des postes et des avantages contre un retour dans l’accord de paix. Des chefs rebelles de l’ASP, comme Arda Hakouma ou Abdoulaye Tago, ont même récemment affirmé que leur objectif final était la prise de Bangui, bien que ces menaces semblent, à ce stade, peu réalistes. 172 Messages écrits et vocaux d’Arda Hakouma et d’Abdoulaye Tago, juillet 2026. Consultés par Crisis Group. Plus les autorités de Bangui tarderont à répondre aux effets déstabilisateurs du conflit soudanais, plus le coût humanitaire, sécuritaire et politique sera élevé pour le pays et sa population. Pour limiter ces risques, le gouvernement centrafricain et ses partenaires devraient agir sur plusieurs fronts. A. Maintenir la réponse humanitaire et désenclaver la Vakaga Tout d’abord, le gouvernement centrafricain devrait s’efforcer de maintenir la réponse humanitaire à son niveau actuel, à défaut de pouvoir la renforcer. Avec l’appui des agences onusiennes et des ONG internationales actives dans la Vakaga, ainsi que des bailleurs de fonds traditionnels du pays comme l’Union européenne (UE), Bangui devrait développer des initiatives socioéconomiques qui bénéficient autant aux réfugiés qu’aux populations locales vulnérables, en particulier dans le domaine de l’agriculture. 173 Ces partenaires pourraient s’inspirer des solutions déployées à l’est du Tchad, où l’UE a par exemple financé la construction de seuils d’épandage permettant d’étendre les surfaces agricoles disponibles. « Tchad : l’UE et le HCR améliorent la production agricole grâce aux seuils d’épandage à Farchana », Alwihda Info , 17 mars 2025. Au-delà de l’urgence, l’Etat centrafricain aurait intérêt à travailler au désenclavement de la zone. La construction de routes, l’une des priorités du plan national de développement 2024-2028, pourrait faire reculer la pauvreté et l’insécurité alimentaire en facilitant le transport des marchandises et en stimulant le commerce entre la région et le reste du pays. 174 « RCA : le plan national de développement (PND) 2024-2028, un nouveau cadre stratégique pour un avenir durable », PNUD, 17 septembre 2024. Des routes bitumées autoriseraient aussi la circulation pendant la saison des pluies et faciliteraient le travail des forces de défense et de sécurité. Elles leur permettraient de patrouiller et d’effectuer des rotations de troupes dans des délais convenables, ce qui contribuerait à améliorer le moral des soldats. L’UE pourrait soutenir cet effort, en contribuant, par exemple, au financement de l’autoroute entre Sibut et Am-Dafock, évoquée plus haut. B. Consolider le dispositif de sécurité et l’accord de paix Pour endiguer la hausse de la criminalité dans la Vakaga, Bangui devrait poursuivre la coopération informelle avec les FSR afin de sécuriser la frontière soudano-centrafricaine. Cette collaboration, engagée en 2024, offre un canal de discussion utile à l’ensemble des parties pour apaiser les tensions et prévenir une escalade en cas d’incidents. Les autorités centrafricaines devraient s’en tenir à leur décision de ne pas formaliser cette coopération pour ne pas légitimer les paramilitaires soudanais et ne pas détériorer davantage la relation entre Bangui et l’armée soudanaise. Elles devraient aussi continuer de limiter cet arrangement à la seule protection de la frontière, afin de ne pas apparaitre comme un soutien des FSR. En parallèle, Bangui devrait poursuivre ses efforts pour préserver l’accord de paix de 2019, ce dernier constituant toujours le cadre de référence pour un retour à la stabilité en RCA. Il devrait assurer sa mise en œuvre avec les groupes qui l’ont réintégré en 2025, en particulier l’UPC, les 3R et le MPC, tout en maintenant ouvertes les négociations avec ceux qui en sont encore absents, comme le FPRC. Les autorités centrafricaines devraient aussi relancer le dialogue avec le Tchad pour clarifier les récentes incompréhensions autour du désarmement des rebelles et réimpliquer N’Djamena dans l’accord. La Minusca et l’UE, qui appuient les programmes de désarmement et de réinsertion, devraient être associées à ces démarches. L’Etat centrafricain gagnerait à intensifier la coopération sécuritaire avec le Tchad pour permettre davantage d’opérations conjointes dans le nord-est du pays. Plus généralement, l’Etat centrafricain gagnerait à intensifier la coopération sécuritaire avec le Tchad pour permettre davantage d’opérations conjointes dans le nord-est du pays. L’armée centrafricaine continuerait ainsi de bénéficier de l’expérience de son homologue tchadienne, mieux aguerrie et équipée. N’Djamena, qui cherche à prévenir les mouvements d’armes et de combattants en provenance du Soudan, bénéficierait autant de ces opérations que la RCA. Enfin, la RCA et ses alliés russes devraient se méfier de l’usage de forces non conventionnelles, comme les « Russes noirs » et les groupes d’autodéfense. Au-delà de l’impunité dont ces miliciens pourraient bénéficier en cas d’exactions contre les civils, leurs opérations risquent de provoquer des réactions violentes des FSR, qui ont déjà attaqué des villages soupçonnés de renseigner les groupes d’autodéfense, et de fragiliser l’accord de paix local d’Am-Dafock. 175 Entretiens de Crisis Group, sources sécuritaires, Vakaga, avril 2026. De plus, même si ces combattants peuvent aider Bangui à mieux contrôler son territoire, leur allégeance n’est pas garantie à long terme. Ils pourraient aisément se retourner contre les autorités si la rébellion armée leur offrait davantage de perspectives ou si l’Etat centrafricain ne satisfaisait pas leurs demandes, à l’instar des miliciens du groupe Azandé Ani Kpi Gbé, anciens alliés du gouvernement dans le sud-est ayant depuis pris les armes contre Bangui. 176 Voir le rapport Afrique de Crisis Group N°319, Centrafrique, les Zandé tiraillés entre armée, milice et troupes russes , 20 novembre 2025. Si l’Etat ne veut pas se passer de ces forces, il devrait au minimum mieux les encadrer, en sanctionnant les dérapages et les actes de prédation. C. Préserver les opérations de la Minusca La Minusca devrait, autant que possible, maintenir une présence robuste dans le nord-est, en particulier dans la Vakaga. Avec le sud-est, cette région est celle qui enregistre aujourd’hui le plus d’incidents violents liés à des groupes armés en RCA. La mission onusienne devrait continuer de soutenir l’accord de paix d’Am-Dafock, en facilitant les réunions entre ses participants, et étudier la possibilité de reproduire cette formule, qui s’est révélée efficace, si des tensions émergent dans d’autres zones. Elle pourrait aussi renforcer la protection physique des réfugiés – quitte à dégarnir ses forces dans d’autres zones moins exposées aux violences – en augmentant ses patrouilles aux abords des sites d’accueil et en renforçant sa capacité de réaction en cas d’alerte. Parallèlement, elle devrait poursuivre ses efforts en faveur du déploiement de l’autorité de l’Etat dans le nord-est du pays. Les Etats membres de l’ONU, qui doivent renouveler le mandat de la Minusca en novembre, devraient tenir compte de la fragilité de la situation actuelle avant d’envisager une réduction du nombre de Casques bleus dans le pays. 177 Briefing de Crisis Group, Dix défis pour les Nations unies en 2026-2027 , op. cit. Les répercussions de la guerre au Soudan mettent non seulement les civils centrafricains en danger, mais risquent aussi de déstabiliser tout le nord-est de la RCA. La Minusca demeure le seul partenaire extérieur de la RCA mandaté pour protéger les civils contre les violences. Dans les régions reculées, les institutions locales dépendent d’elle pour construire et réhabiliter des bâtiments administratifs, bénéficier d’un soutien logistique et assurer la sécurité de leur personnel. Une réduction trop importante de la présence de la Minusca pourrait créer un vide que les groupes rebelles s’empresseraient de combler, risquant de ramener le pays des années en arrière. 178 « Centrafrique : après les élections, consolider les gains sécuritaires », op. cit. En cas de réduction des effectifs de la Minusca, l’Etat centrafricain pourrait renforcer le dispositif sécuritaire dans le nord-est à l’aide des troupes bilatérales prêtées par le Rwanda. Ces dernières sont pour l’instant déployées autour de Bangui et dans le sud du pays, où la situation sécuritaire est aujourd’hui bien plus stable. Elles pourraient envoyer une force d’intervention rapide, idéalement héliportée, dans le nord-est, afin d’être en mesure de réagir rapidement en cas d’incidents sécuritaires. Cette force pourrait se répartir avec Wagner les zones à sécuriser. D. Poser des limites au partenariat avec les EAU Les EAU devraient éviter d’impliquer la RCA dans leur politique au Soudan afin de préserver la fragile sortie de crise centrafricaine. Une dégradation sécuritaire menacerait les investissements déjà effectués par Abou Dhabi dans le pays et réduirait la capacité des entreprises émiraties à exploiter les opportunités économiques locales. La RCA dispose en effet d’un immense potentiel agricole et minier, tandis que sa position au cœur de l’Afrique pourrait lui permettre de devenir un nœud logistique aérien à l’échelle du continent – autant d’atouts susceptibles de servir la stratégie d’investissements des EAU. 179 Les ressources aurifères de la RCA intéressent les EAU, en particulier l’émirat de Dubaï. Elles pourraient en partie compenser la baisse des exportations d’or soudanais vers Dubaï, lesquelles sont passées de 22,2 tonnes en 2024 à 8,2 tonnes en 2025, selon des statistiques officielles de la Banque centrale du Soudan. « Understanding changing gold exports », Sudan Transparency and Policy Tracker, 8 juillet 2026. Les autorités centrafricaines pourraient arguer de leur vulnérabilité particulière vis-à-vis du conflit au Soudan pour dissuader Abou Dhabi d’utiliser le territoire centrafricain pour acheminer des armes aux FSR. Laisser les EAU apporter un soutien aux paramilitaires depuis la RCA expose non seulement le pays à des représailles de l’armée soudanaise, mais ne le protège pas pour autant des violences des FSR dans le nord-est. L’exemple tchadien illustre bien ce risque : les incidents violents impliquant les FSR s’y multiplient, alors même que N’Djamena a autorisé les EAU à approvisionner les FSR depuis son territoire. 180 « L’est du Tchad happé par la guerre au Soudan », op. cit. De plus, à l’inverse du Tchad, la RCA ne dispose pas d’une armée assez forte pour se protéger des débordements du conflit voisin. Les autorités de Bangui pourraient enfin renouer le dialogue avec l’armée soudanaise, en s’appuyant si besoin sur des alliés de Khartoum, tels que l’Arabie Saoudite. De manière générale, diversifier les partenariats afin d’éviter toute situation de dépendance permettrait à la RCA de mieux protéger sa souveraineté. VI. Conclusion Les avancées sécuritaires réalisées par la RCA au cours des dernières années restent fragiles. La guerre au Soudan risque désormais d’inverser cette dynamique en recréant, dans le nord-est du pays, les conditions qui avaient permis aux groupes armés de prospérer au début des années 2010 sous la présidence de François Bozizé : un affaiblissement progressif de l’Etat et un contexte régional propice au renforcement des rebelles. Alors que les combats se poursuivent au Soudan, trois grands dangers guettent la RCA : une circulation accrue de combattants soudanais dans la Vakaga pourrait y aggraver la criminalité et les violences communautaires ; les groupes armés centrafricains pourraient continuer à profiter de l’économie de guerre pour s’enrichir, se réarmer et recruter ; enfin, le rapprochement économique entre la RCA et les EAU, principal parrain des FSR, pourrait exposer le pays à des attaques de l’armée soudanaise. L’histoire récente de la RCA montre que les troubles qui surgissent dans le nord-est n’y restent jamais confinés. Si les tendances actuelles se poursuivent, la région pourrait redevenir un sanctuaire pour les groupes armés et entrainer le pays tout entier dans une nouvelle période d’instabilité. La RCA et ses partenaires disposent toutefois d’une marge de manœuvre pour prévenir ces risques. Malgré les contraintes budgétaires, ils devraient maintenir autant que possible l’aide humanitaire aux réfugiés et investir dans des projets de long terme pour désenclaver la région. Ils devraient aussi y consolider le dispositif de sécurité, y compris en renforçant la coopération militaire entre la RCA et le Tchad et en préservant la présence des Casques bleus, qui jouent un rôle essentiel pour protéger les civils. Les autorités centrafricaines devraient enfin faire preuve de pragmatisme et d’habileté diplomatique. Elles devraient s’adapter aux réalités de la frontière nord, où l’autorité de l’Etat est faible, en poursuivant une collaboration informelle avec les FSR en vue de limiter les déplacements de combattants soudanais en RCA, tout en veillant, malgré l’attrait compréhensible des investissements émiratis, à conserver un statut de neutralité dans le conflit soudanais. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Related Tags Serbia Bosnia And Herzegovina In this episode of War & Peace , guest host Fabienne Hara speaks with Crisis Group’s consulting senior analyst for the Balkans, Marko Prelec, about the elections in Serbia and Bosnia and Herzegovina this month and where both countries might be headed. Don’t Go Backward on China Policy mloukili Thu, 10/29/2026 - 15:33 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Op-Ed / United States 29 October 2026 1 minutes Don’t Go Backward on China Policy Originally published in Foreign Affairs The Folly of a Hawkish Restoration Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Related Tags United States China Nearly halfway through his second term in office, U.S. President Donald Trump has undercut both the United States’ capacity to protect its interests related to China and its role as a provider of regional security in Asia. His undisciplined approach to dealing with Beijing, in which he has focused on building warm personal ties with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and discounted or ignored longstanding sources of tension between the two countries, has reduced Washington’s leverage to shape the relationship. At the same time, Trump’s sustained attacks on allies and partners have driven them to hedge against the United States and strengthen their ties with China. Beijing, in turn, has successfully cast itself as a steady counterweight to an erratic Washington: in 25 of 36 countries that the Pew Research Center surveyed in the spring of 2026—among them Australia, Canada, France, Germany, and Mexico—more respondents had a favorable view of China than of the United States. Given the failures of Trump’s second-term strategy, many Democrats and even moderate Republicans may try to strike more hawkish postures on China after the midterm elections and during the 2028 presidential campaign. This temptation is understandable: there is a strong desire to provide a contrast to a flailing approach and correct what Trump has gotten wrong. But succumbing to it would be dangerous. If Congress and future presidential candidates reflexively adopt a more aggressive stance toward China, they could both undercut a future administration’s capacity to preserve vital diplomatic space with Beijing and further disquiet allies and partners that do not want to be trapped in a new twilight struggle. Overcorrecting Trump’s China policy also would be unlikely to help candidates get elected or boost their public profile in the runup to 2028. Recent polling shows that only a small share of Americans in seven battleground states view China as an enemy or consider it to be one of the top threats to U.S. security. The goal for the next Congress and, eventually, Trump’s successor, should be to prioritize steady competence over performative toughness in dealing with China. Political point scoring and wistful nostalgia for strategies that discount Beijing’s mounting power, and growing domestic support in the United States for great-power calm, would compound Trump’s mistakes rather than mitigate them. A smarter, more coherent China policy—one rooted in disciplined competition with Beijing, patient efforts to build goodwill with anxious allies and partners, and vigorous efforts to refresh the domestic sources of U.S. strength—can make life safer, healthier, and more affordable for Americans. The full article can be read on the Foreign Affairs website. After Serbia’s Election, Foreign Policy Takes a Back Seat, and That’s OK cmoore Thu, 10/29/2026 - 17:58 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Analyst's Notebook / Europe 29 October 2026 2 minutes After Serbia’s Election, Foreign Policy Takes a Back Seat, and That’s OK Crisis Group expert Marko Prelec reflects on the foreign policy implications of Serbia’s recent elections Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Related Tags Serbia Serbia’s election on Sunday 25 October was unprecedented: a non-partisan movement led by university students and their professors toppled an incumbent with a well-oiled patronage machine. The students published a mainly common-sense plan of action heavily focused on cleaning up the state after a decade or more of capture by the outgoing party. Foreign policy statements have, however, made some of Serbia’s neighbours nervous. Start with Kosovo, which Belgrade has long claimed as its own, blocked from UN membership, and sought to manipulate through support for the Kosovo Serb minority. The student movement issued a memorandum in May, calling Kosovo an “inalienable and integral part of the Republic of Serbia” but leavening this by insisting on the need to work “exclusively within the complex currents of the international community”. The plan uses very similar language. The idea that Kosovo is Serbian is a longstanding consensus position in Serbian society, but the students have injected new policy elements that augur well for Kosovo. The movement promises to take apart the patronage machine operating out of the Office for Kosovo and Metohija – ie, the state administration that dispensed hundreds of millions of euros worth of aid to Kosovo Serbs to encourage loyalty to the Serbian List (the only party in Kosovo supported by Belgrade). The List will likely splinter or simply dissolve as a result, leaving Kosovo’s Serbs to organise as they like. The new administration is also unlikely to tolerate figures like Milan Radoičić, who has been indicted for terrorism in Kosovo (he has denied the charges) and is under U.S. sanctions . More broadly, the Vučić regime’s invocation of a “Serbian world” encompassing parts of neighbouring states will likely disappear. The students promise continued support for Serb minorities in Bosnia-Herzegovina, Croatia and Montenegro but without signalling any broader political or territorial agenda. Unlike their predecessors, they do not see the wars of the 1990s as a persistent source of grievance, and have noted that they “should be left to historians”. Serbian politics has been inward focused for years. Vučić made concessions to the EU, for example offering some cooperation on its agenda for Kosovo, and in return Europe overlooked his increasingly authoritarian rule at home. The new government may seek a new bargain, but the new contours of it are not at all clear, and likely won’t be for some time. For now, the students are focused on domestic politics and cleaning house, and Brussels should give them the space to do so, rather than asking them to turn right away to prospects for EU membership. There are some near-term foreign policy priorities – such as maintaining Serbia’s supply of arms and ammunition to Ukraine – which the EU and member states should encourage. Over the longer term, renewing the EU-mediated Kosovo-Serbia dialogue – currently dormant, as neither Vučić nor Kosovo Prime Minister Albin Kurti saw any advantage in compromise – is needed. But Serbia’s friends should give the new government the time and space to develop its own ideas at this promising moment. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc has the largest number of parliamentary seats, at 53, but it is eight short of the 61 needed to govern by itself. Retired general Gadi Eisenkot’s bloc finished second with 48 seats. Crisis Group expert Mairav Zonszein says the biggest story is the huge turnout among Israel’s Palestinian Arab citizens, whose parties reached a record nineteen seats in total. The election is over, but the fight for power has just begun. Netanyahu, who will remain caretaker premier for the time being, could seek to form a coalition with elements of Eisenkot’s camp. Or Eisenkot, though he repeatedly pledged not to do so during the campaign, could cobble together a government with one of the Arab lists. A third scenario – neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot forms a large enough coalition, meaning another round of balloting in a few months’ time – may be the most probable. For more than three decades, a series of UN missions have used their good offices to help repair relations among various political groups amid persistent civil strife. Mogadishu asked this last one to wind down its work as a sign of the country’s progress toward stability. Despite Somalia’s advancements, the UN is leaving at a delicate time, says Crisis Group expert Omar Mahmood. Somalia is in the throes of another political crisis over the timing and format of elections. President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud called for a dialogue with opposition factions on these matters in mid-November, but it will take place without UN behind-the-scenes support to help broker compromise. Discord among politicians in Mogadishu, along with dissension between the federal and several regional governments, is a major reason why the authorities struggle to wear down the Al-Shabaab insurgency that holds swathes of the country’s south. VENEZUELA Opposition politician María Corina Machado made a dramatic return to Venezuela Sunday after ten months abroad. The 2025 Nobel Peace Prize winner got a warm reception as she travelled to Caracas, with tens of thousands cheering as her motorcade passed by. Machado intends to mobilise her supporters to demand an election to replace Delcy Rodríguez, who has been heading an interim government since January, when the U.S. grabbed former President Nicolás Maduro. Crisis Group expert Renata Segura says many Venezuelans, whose living conditions continue to deteriorate, would like to see a vote soon. Last year’s resolution passed 165-7. Washington is seeking to reduce the resolution’s backing as the Trump administration pursues a broader economic pressure campaign on the island (including restrictions on oil shipments and new secondary sanctions). U.S. Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz hosted an event featuring Cuban dissidents, who argued that supporting the resolution excuses the Cuban government’s human rights abuses while obscuring its role in the country’s economic crisis. Cuban diplomats denounced the panel as an attempt to deflect attention from the embargo’s effects. Crisis Group expert Lucian Kim says Zelenskyy’s resistance to U.S. pressure has boosted his approval ratings at home. Unable to go home to Myanmar’s Rakhine State, which is wracked by war, or to work legally in Bangladesh, ever more refugees are trying to escape by boat to Malaysia, Thailand or Indonesia. The new Bangladeshi government should permit Rohingya to secure jobs in sectors with labour shortages. The more ways the Rohingya have to earn a living in refuge, the fewer of them will risk their lives at sea. Wednesday’s meeting among the U.S., Greenland and Denmark in Washington failed to resolve “fundamental disagreement” on Greenland’s future, according to the Danish foreign minister. With Europe already buffeted by Russia's full-scale war in Ukraine, says Crisis Group expert Olga Oliker, this crisis will have dire implications for the future of NATO and European security writ large if the U.S. does not back down. SYRIA Thousands demonstrated in the north east Tuesday against government forces’ expulsion of Kurdish fighters from Aleppo. Since the last Kurdish fighters left the city Sunday, fighting shifted eastward, raising the risk of sustained confrontation. In early January, the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) clashed with the Syrian army in Aleppo as negotiations to integrate Syria’s north east under central government control stalled. Crisis Group expert Nanar Hawach says Damascus cannot take the whole region militarily, but it will likely keep applying pressure on the SDF. The U.S., which supports both sides, has kept a ceiling on escalation thus far and should use its leverage to bring the parties back to the negotiating table. 9 January 2026 CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC Provisional results show that President Faustin-Archange Touadéra has secured a third term after general elections on 28 December. Two challengers – Anicet-Georges Dologuélé and Henri-Marie Dondra – have called for annulling the vote, alleging fraud, while the main opposition coalition boycotted the ballot, citing an uneven playing field. The disputed poll coincided with renewed violence in the south east. Fighters linked to the Azandé Ani Kpi Gbé (AAKG) – a Zandé self-defence militia – disrupted voting in Bambouti. Clashes then spread, including AAKG attacks on government forces around Zémio in early January. The AAKG was initially aligned with Bangui but later broke with the government after its rapprochement with a Fulani-led armed group that the militia accuses of encroaching on Zandé land. Crisis Group expert Fulbert Ngodji says the AAKG may be digging in to battle the state. Stability during Touadéra’s new term will hinge on promoting intercommunal dialogue in the south east, better integrating militias under army command, and reducing regional isolation through development and security reform. IRAN The falling value of Iran's national currency sparked demonstrations that since late December have grown into nationwide anti-regime unrest. The government has altered its subsidy policies but done little to dampen wider grievances. At least three dozen people have been killed as state forces crack down on protests that show little sign of slowing down. Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez says the Islamic Republic faces a major dilemma: it is neither willing nor able to adopt reforms that could meet expectations for political, social and economic change and on notice from U.S. President Donald Trump that outside intervention is possible if its repression intensifies. LEBANON Lebanon said it had passed a milestone in disarming Hizbollah, but the country’s fragile ceasefire deal with Israel remains imperilled. On Thursday, the Lebanese army announced that it had brought all weapons under state control in the southern area between the Litani River and the Israeli border. Israel immediately disputed the army’s assertion, saying Hizbollah retains military infrastructure in that region. Crisis Group expert David Wood says Beirut faces dangers ahead in any case. The army must soon move toward disarming Hizbollah north of the Litani, where the group refuses to comply – driving up the risk of internal discord. Yet Lebanese leaders also know that Israel will almost certainly respond to any hold-ups in disarming Hizbollah with severe military escalations, inflicting still more pain on their embattled country. Brazil: New Evidence of Serious Police Misconduct in Deadly Raid. Play Video Read a text description of this video TEXT ON SCREEN October 28, 2025 Rio de Janeiro, Brazil NARRATION On the morning of October 28th, 2025, hundreds of police officers surrounded two low-income neighborhoods in Rio de Janeiro. By nightfall, the operation would become the deadliest in Brazil's history. TEXT ON SCREEN WARNING. This video contains graphic content, including blurred images of dead bodies. Viewer discretion advised. NARRATION 122 people were killed, including two children and five police officers. According to the autopsy records, over eighty five percent of non-police victims were Black. Police in Rio de Janeiro are required by Supreme Court order to wear body cameras. However, only twenty-three percent of officers wore body cameras that day, and in the footage reviewed by Human Rights Watch, not a single killing was captured on camera. LOWER THIRD Damir Khairat Research Technologist Digital Investigations Lab NARRATION Human Rights Watch was given access to the prosecutor's investigation into the operation, including 8,800 pages of records, 122 autopsies, and nearly 4,000 hours of body camera footage. TEXT ON SCREEN Prosecutors have released the body camera footage shown in this video. Most footage is sealed as evidence and cannot be published. NARRATION Watching all the footage day and night without any breaks would have taken a single researcher almost six months. So, we trained several artificial intelligence models to help us identify the moments that mattered most. First, we needed to organize everything. The models, alongside software that Human Rights Watch developed, synchronized recordings from different officers, mapped their locations, and scanned footage for gunshots and signs of camera tampering. From there we had a searchable platform that let us view the operation as one coordinated event, rather than thousands of separate recordings. What we found was evidence of widespread tampering and obstruction of body cameras. And it consistently happened at the exact moment cameras should have been recording, during arrests, shootouts, or while officers entered homes. Authorities said that the purpose of the raid was to arrest suspected drug traffickers. The evidence we found points to an operation that appeared lethal by design. To explain how we came to this conclusion, let's look at some examples of the moments we trained our AI models to detect. An officer's camera captured this video in an alleyway as a large group of his colleagues pass by, after which the officer quickly covers his camera. He or another officer then flags that there's a camera recording. SOUNDBITE [IN PORTUGUESE] The team has a camera. The team has a camera. No, no I’m talking about the thing there. NARRATION It's unclear why he covered it, but prosecutors later charged him with camera tampering. SOUNDBITE So, this would be the kind of like overall operational view. NARRATION To find incidents like this across almost 4,000 hours of footage from nearly 500 officers, we trained a model to detect similar moments when a camera continued recording, but the lens was covered. Here, an officer is seen struggling to pick the lock on the door of someone's home. Once it's open, he removes his camera and leaves it unattended for over an hour, presumably while he's inside the home. Because the camera was still capturing an image, this recording wasn't initially flagged by our software. So, we trained a second model to identify "stale scenes" where the recording stays the same for long periods of time. As our models learned and improved, they uncovered lots of suspicious recording gaps. In the end, we documented more than 250 camera obstructions. Moments like these are exactly the situations that body cameras are meant to document, helping ensure that any unlawful behavior is captured and that circumstances surrounding the 122 killings can be properly investigated. Another method we used was an AI system that analyzes audio to detect gunshots. After we trained it specifically for Rio police body cameras and local conditions, the model successfully detected most gunshots in a test set of videos. We were also able to use AI to pull text directly from the videos, like the date, time, location and ID number of the officer wearing the camera. But one of the most striking findings came from what we didn't see. Despite the scale of the operation and the number of deaths, we found no footage showing the killings themselves. NARRATION To understand what was missing, we organized body camera recordings across the operation using extracted timestamps. TEXT ON SCREEN Unusable footage Usable footage NARRATION We found that more than half the officers’ recordings had either ended or had significant gaps by noon. From there, the usable footage continued to decline, just as the operation became most deadly. The missing footage, combined with extensive evidence of camera tampering, suggests that body cameras were deliberately misused to prevent killings from being recorded. Throughout our investigation, AI was one tool out of many. Our team of researchers interviewed witnesses in Rio, visited the neighborhood where the killings took place, analyzed police records and autopsies, verified photographs and videos, and manually reviewed AI findings. What AI provided was speed and scale. It helped us process thousands of hours of footage, connect pieces of evidence, and focus our attention where it mattered most. In other words, AI helped us find needles in a very large haystack. Now, it's up to Brazilian prosecutors to thoroughly investigate both the killings and the decisions that led to such a deadly operation. Those who use disproportionate force or misuse body cameras should be held accountable. To learn more about the events of October 28th and Human Rights Watch’s findings, visit HRW.org and read our investigation, A Strategy of Death. Police officers tampered with body cameras and were responsible for serious investigative failures during an operation ostensibly to arrest gang members in a low-income neighborhood in Rio de Janeiro on October 28, 2025. A year-long Human Rights Watch investigation concluded that police breached Supreme Court orders and their own protocols during Operation Containment, which appeared to be lethal by design. Federal and state prosecutors should initiate criminal and civil proceedings to investigate those responsible for abuses, including senior officials and police commanders. (Rio de Janeiro, October 28, 2026) – Police officers tampered with body cameras and failed to take crucial investigative steps during an operation in a low-income neighborhood in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, on October 28, 2025, Human Rights Watch said in an investigation published today. Evidence indicates police used excessive force and may have intentionally killed scores of men and boys. The investigation, “‘A Strategy of Death’: Investigating Brazil’s Deadliest Police Operation,” documents Operation Containment (Operação Contenção), in which a total of 122 people were killed. This included two children and four police officers killed that day, and a fifth police officer who later succumbed to his wounds. An additional two men were killed in the early morning before the official start of the operation. Eighty-five percent of non-police victims of the October 2025 raid were Black. “A Strategy of Death” Investigating Brazil’s Deadliest Police Operation Read the full investigation here None of the killings were captured in the thousands of hours of body camera footage sent by Rio de Janeiro Military Police to the Public Defender’s Office, which Human Rights Watch reviewed after being granted access. “Human Rights Watch processed thousands of hours of body camera footage and analyzed videos, official investigation files, and autopsy records for every victim, yet crucial questions remain because police failed to properly record killings, preserve crime scenes, or collect crucial data,” said Sophia Jones, open source researcher with the Digital Investigations Lab at Human Rights Watch. “The families of those killed, including police officers, deserve answers and accountability with a thorough, independent investigation.” Human Rights Watch interviewed 41 witnesses, family members, and experts, and analyzed 4,400 hours of body camera footage, 9,000 pages of official investigation files, 122 autopsy reports, court records, and hundreds of videos and photographs. Human Rights Watch analyzed the data using several machine learning models built in-house, followed by manual review and assessment by researchers. Based on Human Rights Watch analysis of data from Rio-based security research lab GENI (Grupo de Estudos dos Novos Ilegalismos or Group for the Study of New Illegalities), nongovernmental think tank Fórum Brasileiro de Segurança Pública (Brazilian Public Security Forum), independent security monitoring organization Fogo Cruzado (Crossfire), and media reports, Operation Containment was the deadliest documented one-day police operation in a country where police forces kill more than 6,000 people per year. Human Rights Watch visited the Complexo da Penha, the site of the operation, six months after the raid and found that the criminal group Red Command (Comando Vermelho)—the target of the operation—continued to impose its rule on residents. Despite the stated goal of carrying out 100 arrest warrants for alleged Red Command members, police records show they arrested only 17 of those for whom they had warrants, although it is not clear whether those are the warrants that justified the operation or other pending warrants. Police did not enter the home of the local Red Command leader, for whom they had a warrant, a Civil Police commander told prosecutors, even though body camera footage shows police moving around it. Despite a state law and a Supreme Court order mandating that police wear body cameras, only about 23 percent of the 2,500 civil and military police officers who participated in the raid did, the Rio de Janeiro government said. Machine-Enabled Forensics How Human Rights Watch used Artificial Intelligence to Analyze Body Camera Footage from Rio’s Deadliest Police Raid Read the methodology here Human Rights Watch analysis of the footage of the 527 military police officers who wore the cameras found widespread tampering and obstruction of their use. Officers left cameras running before the operation, effectively draining batteries; covered lenses; placed cameras where they would not capture officers’ actions; and left cameras in vehicles. Such tampering consistently occurred at key moments, during arrests, shootouts, or while officers entered homes, researchers found. Most tampering was on cameras worn by officers whose units engaged in frontline operations, such as the Battalion of Special Police Operations of the Military Police, the unit deployed to the forested area where the majority of killings took place. Researchers determined that 36 percent of gunshot clusters heard on their cameras occurred when the cameras were obstructed. Body camera footage showed officers assaulting and threatening to kill detainees, including a child, whom they forced to lie down next to a dead body while photographing him. In another recording, an officer tells officers to shoot detainees in the legs if they ran. In a third clip, an officer expressed frustration that body cameras prevented them from killing suspects. Researchers also analyzed or verified hundreds of videos and photographs taken by members of the local community that day. In one series of verified videos, officers pile dead bodies, some with their genitalia exposed, into an armored police vehicle, while joking. “Look how wonderful,” one officer said. “We like this.” While police said they spent months planning the operation, there was no evidence that they made any advance preparations to protect crime scenes and conduct forensic analysis. In addition, Civil Police failed to collect basic information for all but two of the 117 non-police victims, such as the names of police officers and residents who brought some of them to a hospital. Only seven suspects were taken to a hospital and subsequently arrested, compared with 117 people killed by police. That unusually high ratio of people killed to people injured (17 to 1) raises serious questions about whether police prioritized lethal force over arresting suspects. An analysis of victim autopsy reports also points in that direction. Over 40 percent of non-police victims in the reports analyzed were shot in the head, over 60 percent were shot four or more times, and nearly 75 percent were shot at least once on the back. One man was shot and then decapitated. According to forensic experts from the Independent Forensic Expert Group of the International Rehabilitation Council for Torture Victims consulted by Human Rights Watch, the evidence suggests that many were targeted and killed intentionally. In many instances, the trajectory of gunshot wounds was from bottom to top, which can be indicative of execution, such as when an individual is shot while lying down or otherwise incapacitated. Brazilian authorities should ensure a thorough and independent investigation into the planning and decisions by senior officials and police commanders that led to the deadly operation. Rio de Janeiro’s new governor, who will take office on January 6, 2027, should introduce a bill to separate forensic services from the Civil Police. “Our investigation shows police flouted the law and their own protocols during the disastrous raid,” said César Muñoz, Brazil director at Human Rights Watch. “Abusive police practices undermine public security by making communities less willing to collaborate with police, while fueling a cycle of violence that endangers both residents and police officers. Brazil needs new effective public security strategies that uphold human rights.”

Alarming Attacks on Women Politicians. Click to expand Image Ana Elisa Santos Silva of the Workers' Party (PT), the youngest federal deputy elected in Minas Gerais state, poses for a photograph in Divinopolis, Brazil, on October 15, 2026. © 2026 Douglas Magno/AFP via Getty Images Overwhelmed by threats—and fearing for her personal safety Satya Rhodes-Conway the current mayor of Madison, Wisconsin in the US, announced on October 23 that she was dropping her bid for reelection. "The price of being in public office has gotten too high,” she said. Globally, women in public life face alarming levels of political violence, including tech-facilitated sexual and gender-based violence, with little protection or recourse. While research finds chillingly high rates of violence against both women and men in politics, women are at greater risk and face more sexualized and gendered violence. After Australian MP Helen Haines was deliberately hit by a car, doctors had to amputate both of her legs. In South Africa, a bloody campaign season included the killing of party activist Jeanette Magugu and a brutal home invasion against mayoral candidate Nhongo Solo. In Brazil, Ana Elisa Santos Silva and other candidates for public office filed police complaints about death and sexual violence threats on the campaign trail; a city councilor, Iara Pimentel, closed her X account due to threats and was hospitalized after a brick hit her at a rally. Bernadette Greene-Placentia, a US congressional candidate in Arizona, reported that she was attacked while repairing campaign posters and raped. While attackers’ motives are often unclear, the result is the same--women and girls who speak up for their communities increasingly experience gendered violence and threats. After a 15-year-old made a video crudely lambasting India’s Prime Minister, she was inundated with rape and death threats. An Iraqi women’s rights leader who challenged an abusive amendment to Iraq’s personal status law was shot dead outside her home. Technological developments also fuel gendered abuses. Of 720 European Parliament members, 46 women and four men had been depicted in or seen their online presence linked to deep fake sexualized images, according to a 2026 study. In the Asia-Pacific region, 18 percent of participating women parliamentarians faced doxing, according to a study. These crimes are taking place amid a global backlash against women’s rights, with political power for women declining in many countries. After years of progress, the percentage of women national cabinet members globally declined to 22 percent in 2026, from 23 percent in 2024. Experts increasingly warn that political violence deters women from running for office. With growing evidence that women’s leadership brings economic and social benefits, we all lose when women are pushed out of politics.

UAE: UN Secretary-General Candidate Whitewashed Abuses. Click to expand Image Lana Zaki Nusseibeh, representative to the United Nations of the United Arab Emirates, speaks during a UN Security Council meeting at UN headquarters on February 23, 2023. © 2023 John Minchillo/AP Photo (Beirut) – Lana Zaki Nusseibeh, a long-serving UAE diplomat and foreign affairs official, has an extensive record of denying and whitewashing the country’s rights abuses in Sudan and Yemen, Human Rights Watch said today. On October 21, 2026, the UAE formally nominated Nusseibeh to be the new United Nations secretary-general. “For years, Lana Nusseibeh has used her position to vehemently deny and divert attention from the UAE’s war crimes in Yemen and support for the abusive Rapid Support Forces in Sudan,” said Bruno Stagno Ugarte, chief advocacy officer at Human Rights Watch. “Her disinformation about the UAE’s rights record, particularly her dismissal of the UN’s own reports documenting the UAE’s links to the RSF, has seriously undermined justice and accountability for the victims.” Nusseibeh has repeatedly denied that the UAE provides military support to the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) in Sudan, while refusing to address clear evidence to the contrary. The RSF, engaged in a conflict with the Sudan Armed Forces (SAF), is responsible for widespread war crimes and crimes against humanity, including as part of a campaign of ethnic cleansing in the Darfur region. The United Nations Fact-Finding Mission on Sudan concluded that their assault on the North Darfur capital of El Fasher “bore the hallmarks of genocide.” In September 2024, Nusseibeh said in a letter to the editor of The Economist that, “[T]he UAE is not providing weapons or any other support to the Rapid Support Forces or any of the warring parties in Sudan.” The letter followed the publication of the first UN Panel of Experts on Sudan’s report, which included conclusions of “credible allegations” that the UAE was providing military support to the RSF through Chad. A UAE government letter from December 2023 in the report annex claims that flights from the UAE to Chad transported humanitarian assistance to Sudanese civilians. The letter is unsigned but bears the letterhead of the Permanent Mission of the UAE to the UN in New York. Nusseibeh was the head of the UAE’s mission from 2013 until April 2024. In April 2024, in response to accusations from the government of Sudan that the UAE was providing the RSF with military, logistical, and political support, Nusseibeh said in a statement that the “claims were baseless” and affirmed the UAE’s categorical rejection “of the false allegations.” In July 2024, asked by CNN whether the UAE was arming the RSF, Nusseibeh replied: “No, those allegations are categorically untrue. The UAE, as it has done in countless places around the world when there is a humanitarian crisis, has projected humanitarian aid in as quickly as possible and then scaled that way.” In November 2025, as a minister of state, Nusseibeh took part in an Emirati “lobbying blitz” with key European Parliament members that said that the UAE was “playing a constructive role in Sudan” in the lead up to a vote on a resolution condemning atrocities in Sudan, according to Politico. The European Parliament passed the resolution without mention of the UAE’s role in the conflict. Several parliamentary sources told Euronews that Nusseibeh “personally lobbied MEPs [members of the European Parliament] in Strasbourg to influence the content of the resolution.” In a subsequent resolution adopted in July 2026, the European Parliament called out the UAE’s role in support of the RSF and requested sanctions on a UAE company involved in the hiring and transfer of mercenaries to the group. A May 2026 Human Rights Watch report found that Colombian private military contractors, apparently hired by a UAE-based company, transited through UAE military bases before being deployed to Sudan to support and fight alongside the RSF, notably during the forces’ takeover of El Fasher, during which the RSF committed multiple massacres, widespread sexual violence, and a massive abduction-for-ransom racket. The findings provide further evidence that the UAE has been assisting or otherwise substantially contributing to the RSF’s capacity to commit war crimes. In August, the Fact-Finding Mission on Sudan released a report echoing these findings, concluding “that individuals and entities operating from, registered in, or linked to the United Arab Emirates played a significant role in networks involved in the recruitment, financing, transportation and deployment of foreign military contractors and the provision of military-related support benefiting the Rapid Support Forces.” The mission noted “several sources” indicating the presence of Colombian fighters in and around El Fasher before, during, and after its takeover. Human Rights Watch has also documented the RSF using military equipment—Serbian-made shells equipping an attack drone—that had first been sold to benefit the UAE armed forces. On October 27, during an interactive dialogue with UN member states and civil society organizations, Nusseibeh was asked about her denials of findings by the Panel of Experts on Sudan and the Fact-Finding Mission. She did not respond directly to a question about whether she would “continue to reject the findings of the very organization [she] seeks to lead.” Instead, she stated that she had taken a leave of absence from her post as a UAE minister and would refer any questions about the UAE to the UAE government. As permanent representative to the UN, Nusseibeh repeatedly defended the UAE as complying with international law during its intervention in Yemen while dismissing evidence of widely documented abuses. Beginning in March 2015, the UAE played a prominent role in a coalition of countries that conducted military operations in Yemen, including by committing over 30 fighter jets to carry out airstrikes, providing naval ships to enforce the coalition’s maritime blockade, and supporting abusive local forces. In 2016, Human Rights Watch documented 58 unlawful Saudi/UAE-coalition airstrikes, killing nearly 800 civilians and hitting homes, markets, hospitals, schools, businesses, and mosques, and the coalition's use of cluster munitions. In August 2016 and May 2018, Nusseibeh issued statements defending UAE actions in Yemen, claiming that the UAE “takes its own responsibility for upholding international humanitarian law and for protecting civilians very seriously.” The 2018 statement was made a few months before the UAE ordered humanitarian organizations in the coastal city of Hodeida to evacuate despite the immense humanitarian needs, while the Saudi/UAE-led coalition sought to take control of the city from the Houthis. In 2021, the UAE, alongside Saudi Arabia, successfully led a lobbying campaign to end the mandate of the Group of Eminent Experts, an international, impartial, and independent body the Human Rights Council had established to report on rights violations and abuses in Yemen. “Lana Nusseibeh has spent over a decade in roles acting for the UAE government and repeatedly whitewashing their abusive role in Yemen and Sudan, presenting Abu Dhabi as a humanitarian actor while dismissing or obscuring mounting evidence of its role in fueling abuses,” Stagno Ugarte said. “Having dismissed and undermined the findings of the UN’s own reports, UN member states should be asking tough questions about Nusseibeh’s willingness to defend the independence and integrity of the UN and its investigative mechanisms, including those exposing UAE abuses, at a time when these institutions are under attack.”

No Accountability One Year After Tanzania Election Violence. Click to expand Image Protesters use different materials to build barricades and block a road as clashes erupt in Dar es Salaam during Tanzania's presidential elections on October 29, 2025. © 2025 AFP by Getty Images One year after Tanzania’s contested 2025 elections, authorities have yet to make any arrests for human rights violations committed before and during the vote. In the months leading up to the elections, the government intensified its repression of the political opposition, government critics, and the media. Authorities also failed to account for a spate of apparent enforced disappearances, including that of former Tanzanian ambassador to Cuba Humphrey Polepole, who was reported missing just weeks before the elections. Polepole had publicly criticized the ruling party, Chama Cha Mapinduzi, for not being “aligned with safeguarding human rights, peace, and respect for people.” His whereabouts remain unknown. On and after election day, police and people in plainclothes killed hundreds of protesters and bystanders in response to widespread protests and while enforcing a five-day nationwide lockdown. A year on, the fate of many remains unknown as families have reported burying their relatives with no body. Authorities also arrested over 2,000 people they accused of destroying government property and of treason during this period, but later released some. Some, including those interviewed by Human Rights Watch, said police beat them while falsely accusing them of participating in the protests. In November 2025, President Samia Suluhu Hassan established a commission of inquiry to investigate the violence. It concluded that at least 518 people were killed but failed to meaningfully scrutinize the role of security forces. The president has since established another commission that will reportedly investigate the planning of the unrest and excessive and unlawful use of force during the elections. However it remains unclear whether this includes investigating and ensuring the prosecution of people responsible for security force abuses. Meanwhile, the authorities have intensified their crackdown on government critics in recent months. The treason trial of Tundu Lissu, the leader of the main opposition party, Chama Cha Demokrasia Na Maendeleo (CHADEMA), continued this year. On October 21, authorities charged John Pambalu, a CHADEMA official, with treason for allegedly forming an “intention to persuade the public to cause obstruction” of the elections through protests. Treason carries the death penalty in Tanzania. A year since the election violence, families of those killed or missing are still waiting for answers and justice. President Hassan’s government should stop targeting critics and instead ensure credible investigations into disappearances and security force abuses and hold those responsible to account.

Indonesia: Landmark Ruling Allows Civilian Trials of Soldiers. Click to expand Image The Constitutional Court of Indonesia, in Jakarta, October 2023. © 2023 Yasuyoshi Chiba/AFP via Getty Images (London) – The Indonesian Constitutional Court’s ruling requiring reform of the military justice system so that military personnel accused of ordinary crimes can be tried in civilian courts is a major step for justice in Indonesia, Human Rights Watch said today. The government should immediately revise the 1997 Military Justice Law, which has long prevented civilian prosecutions of members of the armed forces for crimes under the Indonesian criminal code, including for serious human rights violations. On October 15, 2026, the Constitutional Court’s nine justices unanimously ruled that the Military Justice Law is conditionally unconstitutional under articles 24(1) and 28D(1) of the 1945 Constitution, which guarantee an independent judiciary and equality before the law. The law will become unconstitutional if it is not amended by October 2028, giving the government a two-year deadline. “The Constitutional Court’s landmark ruling recognizes that Indonesia’s military courts aren’t capable of impartially trying crimes against civilians, as victims and human rights defenders have said for decades, ” said Elaine Pearson, Asia director at Human Rights Watch. “President Prabowo Subianto and the Indonesian parliament should consult with victims and rights groups and promptly amend the military justice law.” Under the 1997 law, civilian police cannot investigate military personnel, with only a few rarely invoked exceptions. Even when soldiers serving in civilian institutions have been accused of crimes under the criminal code, military courts have had jurisdiction over the case. Human Rights Watch found that Indonesia’s military justice system lacks transparency, independence, and impartiality, and has failed to properly investigate and prosecute alleged serious human rights abuses by military personnel. The petitioners challenged articles 9(1), 43(3), and 127 of the law, which allow active duty military personnel to be tried in military courts even for crimes ordinarily prosecuted in civilian courts. The Constitutional Court found that the distinction between military offenses and ordinary criminal offenses must be clearly defined. Justice Enny Nurbaningsih said that when an offense has no military character but accountability for it remains within a command-based system, “there is a structural risk that military’s institutional interests will conflict with the need to ensure independent and impartial legal proceedings.” The Constitutional Court also noted that the military judiciary is not fully integrated into the judicial system overseen by the Supreme Court and urged lawmakers to create a single system. Military judges are active duty soldiers, and investigation, prosecution, and adjudication all take place within the military chain-of-command. Revisions to the Military Justice Law have been pending for decades. As part of structural reforms that followed the end of authoritarian rule under President Soeharto from 1965 to 1998, the 2004 Armed Forces Law made soldiers subject to civilian courts for ordinary crimes. However, that provision would only take effect when a new military justice law was enacted. The Constitutional Court’s ruling imposes a two-year time frame for those revisions, which successive Indonesian governments have deferred. Muhammad Afif Abdul Qoyim, a lawyer from the Indonesian Legal Aid Foundation, told Human Rights Watch: “There is no need to wait two years to revise the Law on Military Justice so that new rules are in line with the Constitutional Court’s ruling.” Serious abuses by Indonesian security forces have gone unpunished for decades because of legal restrictions on civilian investigations and prosecutions under the 1997 law, Human Rights Watch said. On March 12, 2026, military personnel carried out an acid attack against Andrie Yunus, a 27-year-old deputy coordinator at KontraS (Commission for the Disappeared and Victims of Violence), causing burns over 24 percent of his body and possible loss of sight in his right eye. A military court in Jakarta convicted four soldiers in June and sentenced them to 18 months to three years in prison and dismissal from the military. On August 20, a military appeals court reduced the two longest sentences by six months each and overturned their dishonorable discharges. The Judicial Commission has alleged ethical violations by the panel that tried the case at first instance. KontraS said in a statement that the Constitutional Court ruling “closes a legal loophole that has been seen as shielding errant soldiers from accountable law enforcement, and marks a new chapter in upholding the rule of law and completing the mandate of security sector reform in Indonesia.” One of the petitioners in the case is the mother of a 15-year-old boy tortured to death in Medan, North Sumatra, in 2024 by a soldier who was sentenced by a military court to only 10 months in prison, though the maximum penalty is 15 years. In Papua, the military justice system has repeatedly failed victims of violence allegedly committed by military personnel. Under President Prabowo Subianto, a former general dismissed from the military for human rights violations, the military’s role in civilian affairs has expanded. In March 2025, the national legislature passed amendments to the Armed Forces Law to allow active duty officers to hold more government posts. The number of civilian institutions open to serving soldiers—which includes the Supreme Court and the Attorney General’s office—rose from 10 to 14. Lawmakers should prioritize amending the Military Justice Law through an open process with meaningful participation of victims and civil society, Human Rights Watch said. The amended law should clarify investigative and prosecutorial powers and provide a mechanism for transferring cases from military courts to the civilian system. “Justice for civilian victims of military abuses shouldn’t be blocked by an unfair military court system,” Pearson said. “Amending the law on military justice will support efforts begun decades ago to ensure the Indonesian military is a professional, credible institution whose soldiers are held accountable when they commit serious abuses.”

Niger: Prominent Journalist ‘Disappeared’ for 2 Months. Click to expand Image Nigerien journalist Moussa Kaka, former correspondent for Radio France Internationale, February 12, 2007. © 2007 Seyllou/AFP via Getty Images (Nairobi) – Niger’s authorities should urgently disclose the whereabouts of the prominent journalist Moussa Kaka, who was forcibly disappeared two months ago, Human Rights Watch said today. They should ensure his safety and release him unless he has been charged with a valid criminal offense. On August 31, 2026, Kaka, the director-general of Radio Télévision Saraounia and a former correspondent for Radio France Internationale (RFI), left his office in Niamey, the capital, to return home but never arrived, raising immediate concerns. For weeks, his family and colleagues were not able to obtain information about his whereabouts. On September 25, during Niger’s Universal Periodic Review at the United Nations in Geneva, Justice Minister Alio Daouda acknowledged that Kaka was being detained. The minister said Kaka was being held for an alleged “offense” and would “answer before the courts,” but provided no details about the accusation or his place of detention. “Two months after Moussa Kaka vanished in Niger, the authorities have yet to provide his location or explain his detention,” said Ilaria Allegrozzi, senior Sahel researcher at Human Rights Watch. “Kaka’s family will continue to grapple with the uncertainty until the authorities resolve his disappearance.” Kaka is a respected figure in African investigative journalism. For years, he reported for RFI in Niger, until the military junta suspended its broadcasts in 2023. Throughout his career, he has continued his work under successive governments despite the risks and repeated detentions for his journalism. In September 2007, under then-President Mamadou Tandja, the authorities arrested Kaka and accused him of links to ethnic Tuareg rebels, following his extended coverage of the Tuareg rebellion in northern Niger. He spent 379 days in prison before being released in October 2008 following a sustained national and international campaign for his freedom.
